Abstract.

In large-scale payment networks, entities (card, merchant, etc.) and their
interactions play a key role in transaction anomaly detection. However,
transaction patterns between different entities usually change more frequently
than the production model refresh schedule. Meanwhile, entity embedding tables
suffer from high-cardinality and sparse interaction issues. To
resolve the above challenges, we present PersonaAgent, an agentic
transaction anomaly detection framework which represents the latest entity
behavior signals as personas and saves them in a refreshable memory. Offline, a
weekly scheduled batch job is used to extract the latest behavior signals and
update them in the memory. At inference time, a lightweight adapter retrieves the
corresponding entity behavior signals of each transaction from memory and uses
them to augment the base anomaly classifier’s scoring. Through comprehensive
benchmarking with different anomaly detection models at Visa, PersonaAgent is
able to score transactions efficiently (a 1,000-transaction CPU batch in
1–2 ms), lifting the PR-AUC by 0.65–6.58% and the production business metric
by 8.93–14.24% relatively in deployment.

Keywords: transaction anomaly detection, retrieval-augmented scoring,
semantic persona memory, agentic workflow

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text:
In fiscal year 2025, Visa reported 4.9B credentials and 175M+ merchant locations
across 200+ countries and territories. Visa-branded payment and cash
transactions totaled 329B that year, including those processed by other
networks (Visa Inc., 2025). Transaction anomaly detection at this scale
requires Visa’s detection models, which we call detectors, to score each
authorization within a tight latency budget
despite rare anomalies, concept drift, and delayed
labels (Lucas and Jurgovsky, 2020; Pang et al., 2021; Gama et al., 2014).
Much of the evidence for an anomaly comes from context: the card’s spending
history, merchant behavior, merchant category code (MCC), and location. Payment
systems therefore model entity histories, peer cohorts, and
relations (Yeh et al., 2020b; Xiao et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2022). Joint context also
matters: an MCC that appears unremarkable in aggregate can behave differently
within one location. Transaction foundation models use large-scale
pretraining (Dou et al., 2025; Yeh et al., 2026), building on earlier
sequential tabular transformers (Padhi et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023). These
advances increase what a detector can represent, but do not necessarily shorten
its release cycle.

Industrial detectors such as Visa’s are large models. Each release
requires integration and validation (Sculley et al., 2015), so a detector’s
update cycle typically lasts at least several months. Entity behavior drifts
much faster; in the setting we study, it can be re-estimated weekly, so the
knowledge encoded in a deployed detector’s parameters falls behind. We call this
difference a knowledge-latency gap (Fig. 1).
Closing the gap requires behavior evidence that generalizes beyond individual
identifiers and can be refreshed without changing detector weights. Entity
embedding tables (Chen et al., 2019), the common way to learn entity
behavior and interactions, provide limited evidence for rare entities, even less
for entity combinations such as MCC–Location pairs, and none for unseen IDs;
semantic initialization enriches such embeddings (Fan et al., 2025), but
they remain part of the detector’s weights, so updating them still requires a
new release. Feature stores serve refreshed aggregates for individual entities
but leave two questions open: which behavior signals describe an entity, and how
entities with similar behavior should be grouped so that long-tail entities,
whose own evidence is scarce, can borrow from their group. Hand-written rules
and feature-engineering pipelines rely on people to answer these questions
across millions of Merchants, 800+ MCCs, and 230+ Location codes, while
clustering numerical features alone
groups entities by value similarity rather than by what their behavior means.
Large language model (LLM) agents can answer these questions instead: through
self-evolution, they find semantic topics, groups of entities with
similar behavior, and the behavior features that describe them, keeping only
revisions that
improve held-out development performance. Calling an LLM for each transaction
during online scoring
(inference) (Tan et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026; Kath et al., 2026),
however, would put text generation on the latency-critical path. These
observations lead to our design: agents learn offline what personas should
capture, and a lightweight adapter injects them into each frozen detector
online.

Following this design, we present PersonaAgent, an agentic
framework that stores refreshable multi-entity behavior outside frozen detectors
in Semantic Persona Memory. A persona is an auditable behavior
record of an entity, group, or supported interaction at a cutoff time.
PersonaAgent uses LLM agents only at design time: an LLM selects salient
signals from
many candidates and describes them in grounded narratives that use a
shared behavioral vocabulary. These narratives organize the selected numerical
signals with their temporal and peer-group context, helping agents compare
entity behavior. A narrative schema ties each claim to a declared field, window,
baseline, and support value. An example sentence, with numerical details
omitted, reads: “Over the declared window, this Merchant’s cross-location
activity is above its peer-group baseline and its recent transaction size above
its own prior level.” The agents search for a persona protocol
specifying the signals, narrative schema, and rules for grouping MCCs,
Locations, and Merchants with similar behavior into semantic topics.
Three LLM roles propose revisions, while a fourth, the Protocol Critic,
diagnoses each candidate. Agents use MCC and Location narratives and their
embeddings to formulate MCC and Location topics, with behavior-feature
clustering forming Merchant topics within the MCC topics. Adapter performance on
a development set, held out from all evaluation data, guides revisions to
this hierarchical construction; a prespecified rule selects the protocol to
freeze (Section 4.1). The resulting semantic topics outperform
matched conventional clustering in standalone prediction for three of four group
views (Section 5.3). A weekly refresh then applies the frozen
protocol to eligible history, updating numerical records under its fixed topic
definitions without an LLM or further revision, while online scoring
reads the active validated memory. SR-Fraud (Tan et al., 2026a) also uses LLM
agents to adapt detection to changing payment behavior, but calls an LLM at
scoring time to make decisions on transactions. PersonaAgent keeps every
LLM call offline to meet Visa’s efficiency and determinism requirements.

The five persona views cover the Card Spending Behavior Summary (spending
summary), Merchant topics, MCC topics, Location topics, and supported
MCC-topic–Location-topic interactions. Deterministic lookup by key (the
card, a topic, or a topic pair) and fallback supply one record per view. A
lightweight, detector-specific, tree-based adapter then computes the final
score: five encoders, one per view, turn each view’s record into an anomaly
prediction, and
a small neural network fuses these predictions with the detector’s own score and
its metadata-adjusted version (Section 4.3). Only the adapter is
fitted; the detector’s weights stay unchanged, so new behavioral evidence
reaches each detector without waiting for its next release
(Fig. 2). We evaluate four frozen detectors in a held-out
offline test (Period 1) and a post-launch deployment (Period 2), where live
traffic was scored before outcomes were known. PersonaAgent goes live as a
release package: one memory snapshot, the detector-specific adapters that
read it, and release metadata recording their versions. A package is validated
and activated as a whole, so each adapter always reads memory with the schema
and topics it was fitted on. Both periods used the same, unchanged package.
Matched ablations, refit without persona views and evaluated on independent test
data, show the contribution of persona evidence beyond added adapter capacity.
Our contributions are as follows:

•

We introduce PersonaAgent, an agentic framework for transaction
anomaly detection that stores multi-entity behavioral evidence in refreshable
Semantic Persona Memory. LLM agents design the persona protocol offline,
while memory can be refreshed independently of detector parameters.

•

We develop a lightweight retrieval-augmented scoring method that
enables multiple frozen detectors to use shared persona memory. The method
combines retrieved behavioral evidence with existing detector scores without
changing detector parameters or calling an LLM online.

•

We evaluate PersonaAgent through a held-out offline test and a
post-launch deployment at Visa. Across four detectors, it achieves an
8.93–14.24% relative improvement in the production business metric (BM1)
during deployment.

sections.name: Transaction representations.
sections.text:
Transaction foundation models and sequential tabular transformers learn
temporal representations from event histories
(Dou et al., 2025; Yeh et al., 2026; Skalski et al., 2023; Padhi et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023).
Graph models and embedding tables for entities or peer cohorts encode
relationships
(Rao et al., 2022; Dou et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2023; Yeh et al., 2020a),
while payment-network studies incorporate merchant history
(Yeh et al., 2020b). LLM-based sentence embeddings can also initialize
entity embeddings, enriching representations within the model
(Fan et al., 2025).
Transaction anomaly detection operates under extreme
class imbalance, with confirmed anomalies far rarer than other transactions
(Lucas and Jurgovsky, 2020; Pang et al., 2021). Related work examines anomaly detection in
financial data and general time series
(He et al., 2021; Paoletti et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025), label delay in financial
prediction (Sarig et al., 2025), and forecasting or imputation under missing or
shifting observations
(Yeh et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2026a; Hu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025b).
PersonaAgent pools evidence for low-volume Merchants in behavior-derived
topics, applies minimum-support requirements to group records, and routes
previously unseen Merchants through a predefined parent MCC-topic fallback.
This is related to hierarchical smoothing for high-cardinality categorical
attributes with many distinct values, where a rarely seen value borrows
statistics from its parent group (Micci-Barreca, 2001).

sections.name: Retrieval-augmented scoring.
sections.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a language model’s output in documents
retrieved from an external corpus (Lewis et al., 2020), while tabular
retrieval methods use similar rows (nearest neighbors) as additional context
for prediction (Qin et al., 2021; Gorishniy et al., 2024). BRIGHT separates batch
computation of entity embeddings from real-time prediction within one model
(Lu et al., 2022). The post-hoc calibration methods in
(Guo et al., 2017; Kull et al., 2019) align predictions with observed outcome
rates using only the trained model’s output at scoring time. PersonaAgent
retrieves numerical behavioral context from shared, refreshable multi-entity
memory and combines it with each frozen detector’s score through a
lightweight, detector-specific adapter. Deterministic key lookup with
predefined fallback serves records built offline, so online scoring requires
no similarity search or generation. The memory and compatible adapters are
validated and released as one versioned package, allowing behavioral evidence to be
updated independently of detector weights.

sections.name: Agentic design and optimization.
sections.text:
LLM-based optimizers refine instructions and structured pipelines
(Khattab et al., 2024; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025).
CAAFE retains LLM-proposed features only when they improve validation
performance (Hollmann et al., 2023), while FeatLLM constructs features offline
so that inference needs no LLM query (Han et al., 2024). LLMs can also induce
interpretable topics or clusters from text (Pham et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023)
or assign retrieval tags (Tang et al., 2025). LLM agents forecast time series
(Yeh et al., 2025), and a recent survey identifies memory and knowledge
as one capability layer in agentic time-series systems (Hu et al., 2026).
TimeEvo turns a time-series agent’s diagnosed failures into new tools and
accepts tool-library revisions only if they pass a paired validation
check (Yang et al., 2026b). PersonaAgent iteratively refines a persona protocol
at design time, with proposal roles suggesting revisions and a Protocol Critic
diagnosing each candidate. This bounded protocol self-evolution determines how
shared, versioned multi-entity memory is built and used by several frozen
detectors. Because LLM evaluators can differ systematically when judging the same evidence under a common rubric
(Wang et al., 2026), acceptance follows a prespecified development
rule: a candidate is accepted only when development BM1 improves and the
required checks pass.

sections.name: Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
sections.text:
A transaction x occurs at event time t(x) , but its outcome
y(x)\in\{0,1\} may not be known until much later. Here, y(x)=1 denotes a
confirmed anomaly under the confidential labeling policy. Each snapshot of
Semantic Persona Memory (Section 4.2) is built from
transactions observed by a cutoff time T and may use an outcome only if it
was available by T ; we call evidence available by T cutoff-valid.
We score x using the release package (memory with compatible adapters) that
was active at its event time t(x) , even if the request is processed later.
Its memory was built at a cutoff T(x)<t(x) using only evidence available by
T(x) ; applying the same rule in offline evaluation therefore prevents scores
from using outcomes learned after the memory cutoff.

A detector is a base classifier that scores a transaction from the
transaction’s own features. We refer to the four proprietary detectors as
Detectors 1–4. Detector  m is a frozen function f_{m} with base score
s_{\mathrm{base}}(x)=f_{m}(x)\in[0,1] , where higher means more anomalous; we
treat it as a black box and keep it fixed.

sections.name: Problem.
sections.text:
For each detector  m , we fit a lightweight adapter that computes a final
anomaly score s_{\mathrm{final}}(x) using three types of information: the
frozen base score s_{\mathrm{base}}(x) , the cutoff-valid persona records for
x in the memory built at T(x) , and a metadata input derived from a
predefined transaction metadata field (Section 4.3).
Our goal is to improve anomaly detection performance, as measured by the
metrics below, while keeping f_{m} unchanged and ensuring that retrieval
and scoring are deterministic and meet the online latency requirement.

We report BM1, the production business metric at the deployed operating
point, together with PR-AUC and AUC; higher is better for all three. Because
the definition of BM1 and all absolute metric values are confidential, we
report each metric’s relative improvement over the frozen detector. For BM1, this is
\Delta\mathrm{BM1}=(\mathrm{BM1}_{\mathrm{final}}-\mathrm{BM1}_{\mathrm{base}})/\mathrm{BM1}_{\mathrm{base}} ;
\Delta PR-AUC and \Delta AUC are defined likewise, and a relative improvement of +10\%
means 1.1 times the base metric value.

sections.name: Method
sections.text:
PersonaAgent has three core parts, one for each stage in
Fig. 2: agentic persona-protocol self-evolution, Semantic
Persona Memory, and a tree-based adapter for each detector. At design
time
(Section 4.1), LLM roles propose changes to a persona protocol,
and a prespecified rule selects the protocol to freeze. At each weekly
refresh (Section 4.2), a batch job applies the frozen
protocol to cutoff-valid history and builds a new memory snapshot, which can
be activated only after validation, together with compatible adapters in one
release package. At scoring time (Section 4.3), each
detector’s adapter reads five numerical records from the active package and
uses them with the frozen base score and metadata input to compute the final
score. The LLM is used only at design time; the weekly build and online scoring
follow the fixed protocol, and scoring is deterministic. Release controls,
fallback rules, and pseudocode are given in
Appendices B, C,
and E, respectively.

sections.name: Agentic Persona-Protocol Self-Evolution
sections.text:
At design time, the agents define how persona memory is built and used during
scoring. These rules form the persona protocol, which has five parts:
the behavior signals to compute; the narrative schema, which specifies how
narratives are written; topic construction, which groups MCCs, Locations, and
Merchants with similar measured behavior into semantic topics; the
retrieval rules for looking up records and choosing fallbacks; and the release
checks a build must pass. Appendix Table 7 gives an
example of each.
To compare measured behavior when defining MCC and Location topics, the agents
use grounded narratives produced under the protocol’s narrative schema. For
each narrative, the LLM selects 4–6 numerical behavior signals that it
considers important or indicative of changes in behavior. The schema requires
each claim to name its numerical field, history window, baseline, and support
value (the amount of supporting history). These numerical details constrain
what the narrative can claim while the LLM chooses which behaviors to
emphasize.

The protocol is refined and selected through a protocol search that
ends before either reported period and uses a separate development set,
with no data from either period. One LLM performs four offline roles, with a
separate prompt for each role (Fig. 2(A)). The Signal
Definition, Narrative Schema, and Topic Rule roles propose changes to the
behavior signals, narrative schema, and topic construction, respectively. In
round  j , these changes are combined into one candidate protocol \Pi_{j} .
For each candidate, the system rebuilds memory and fits a temporary adapter for
Detector 4, after which the development evaluation reports development BM1
and check results. Source-consistency checks flag narrative values that do not
match the aggregates they were based on. To guide the next revision, the fourth
role, the Protocol Critic, reviews these flagged values and development BM1.
Its feedback can also lead to changes in the retrieval rules and release
checks.
Under the fixed selection rule, a candidate replaces the current best protocol
only when development BM1 improves and the required checks pass. The
development evaluation, selection rule, and search budget (the maximum number
of candidates) are fixed before the search starts (Algorithm 1).
Section 5.2 tests whether the selected protocol transfers to
Detectors 1–3.

The Topic Rule role proposes a hierarchical topic scheme
in which the agents interpret MCC and Location narratives and their embeddings
to select which MCCs and Locations belong to each topic. The embeddings are
numerical vectors that place similar narratives close together
(Fig. 3). Within each MCC topic, behavior-feature
clustering groups Merchants with similar behavior into Merchant topics at
design time. For example, under one MCC topic, separate Merchant topics
describe predominantly online domestic activity and predominantly online
cross-location activity. Because each candidate’s development results guide the
next revision, the MCC and Location topics result from multi-agent
self-evolution rather than a single clustering pass.
Section 5.3 compares the resulting topic scheme with matched
conventional clustering of numerical features. When the search ends, the
selected protocol \Pi^{\star} , including its topic definitions, is frozen
together with an execution configuration that records the software and
execution settings.

sections.name: An example topic.
sections.text:
The MCC topic for airline and cruise
travel provides a concrete example, with a narrative that describes behavior
pooled across its member MCCs. With numerical details omitted here, it reports
average transaction size, card-not-present share, and cross-location share above
their overall baselines, and approval rate below its baseline.
Appendix D illustrates a possible protocol revision
using this example. Scoring reads the topic’s numerical record, not the
narrative, and the weekly build recomputes this record from eligible history
under the same topic definition. The adapter can use this record to score a
purchase at a cruise line the memory has never seen, a previously unseen
Merchant. The purchase’s MCC still identifies this topic even when the cruise
line has no supported Merchant-topic mapping. Section 4.3
follows this purchase through scoring.

sections.name: Semantic Persona Memory Refresh
sections.text:
With the protocol frozen, weekly builds update the numerical records in
Semantic Persona Memory. Each record stores behavior statistics for one card,
semantic topic, or supported MCC-topic–Location-topic pair, and its key
identifies that card, topic, or pair. A Merchant-topic record, for example,
contains statistics such as the topic’s cross-location share. The record is
computed from eligible transactions observed by cutoff T , using only outcomes
available by T , and its support measures how much eligible history was
used. Support decides whether a group has enough history for its own record and
tells the adapter how reliable the record is. Each versioned memory snapshot
contains these records and the maps that assign Merchants, MCCs, and Locations
to their topics.

The memory has five views (Table 1). The spending
summary records twelve months of the card’s behavior, including how its
activity is distributed across Merchant, MCC, and Location topics, while the
Merchant, MCC, and Location views summarize behavior in the topics assigned to
the transaction’s Merchant, MCC, and Location. The interaction view records how
an MCC-topic–Location-topic pair differs from its separate MCC and Location
patterns.
Topic records combine history across their members, providing statistics for
entities with little or no history of their own. Unlike the per-card spending summaries, group records are
kept for 56 Merchant topics instead of millions of Merchant keys, 19 MCC topics
instead of 800+ MCCs, nine Location topics instead of 230+ Location codes, and
at most 19\times 9=171 topic pairs instead of 184,000+ potential
MCC–Location code pairs.

Because an MCC topic can behave differently across Location topics, we keep
a separate record for each supported MCC-topic–Location-topic pair.
Figure 4 illustrates this variation in one offline
snapshot. Section 5.3 tests whether the interaction view predicts anomalies on
its own.

The weekly build. Each week, the batch job (Fig. 2(B))
uses eligible historical transactions observed by that week’s cutoff T and
outcomes available by T . It applies the selected protocol \Pi^{\star} and its
execution configuration to recompute all five numerical views (Appendix C). Topics
are settled at design time: the build updates the aggregated feature values
under those topics and maps new Merchants or codes to existing topics by the
fixed topic-assignment rules. Narratives and
embeddings are produced only at design time and are never read during scoring.
The serving memory contains numerical records and their source metadata, and
the weekly build calls no LLM.
Before activation, each build must pass compatibility checks on schema and
topic identity; a failed build leaves the previously validated package active
(Appendix B).

sections.name: Online Adapter Scoring
sections.text:
All detectors use the same memory, but their scores are on different scales.
Each detector therefore has its own adapter, a lightweight model (tree-based encoders and a small neural network) that
combines its base score with information from the retrieved persona
records and
the metadata input to compute a final score (Fig. 2(C)); the
detector itself is never changed. Scoring retrieves one persona record per view,
forms the adapter’s inputs, and runs the adapter.

Retrieving persona records. The card’s own key selects its spending
summary, the topic-assignment maps
assign the transaction’s Merchant, MCC, and Location to their topics, and the
pair of MCC and Location topics forms the interaction key. Exact-key lookup then
returns one numerical record per view, so the number of retrievals is fixed and
scoring involves no nearest-neighbor search or topic construction. When a
Merchant has no supported topic mapping or a group has too little history for
its own record, a predefined fallback record from a
larger group fills the view (Appendix C).

Adapter inputs. From each record, the adapter takes a fixed set of
numerical fields, including behavior values and reliability indicators such as
support and fallback level. Together with three activity shares from the
spending summary (the card’s shares of eligible historical activity in the
transaction’s Merchant, MCC, and Location topics), these fields form the
persona feature vector, whose length is fixed regardless of how many
cards and Merchants the memory covers
(Appendix C). The system computes the
metadata input by comparing a predefined transaction metadata field with
a memory-derived Merchant-topic reference.

The example purchase. For the cruise purchase of Section 4.1, the MCC maps to the
airline-and-cruise topic and the Location to a Location topic, which together
give its interaction key; the cruise line itself has no supported mapping to a
Merchant topic. The MCC view therefore reads the airline-and-cruise topic’s
record, and the Merchant view uses the parent MCC-topic fallback record for the
same topic. In the persona feature vector, the MCC share is the card’s share of
eligible historical activity in the airline-and-cruise topic, or 0 if the card
has none there; the Merchant share is marked missing, not replaced by the MCC
share. Section 5.5 shows that PersonaAgent’s gain holds on transactions served
by MCC-topic fallback, such as this one.

Adapter model. Five tree-based encoders, one per persona view, handle
the different fields and missing values across views.
Each encoder takes the features of one view and produces an anomaly prediction
between 0 and 1; the spending-summary encoder also uses the three activity shares.
The metadata input enters the adapter only through the
metadata-adjusted base score \widetilde{s}_{\mathrm{base}}(x) .
The fusion network \operatorname{Fuse} , a small multilayer perceptron (MLP)
with hundreds of parameters, models interactions among the five view predictions, the base score, and the
metadata-adjusted base score to compute the final score
(Appendix B):

where each u is the prediction from one view, with subscripts \mathrm{cb} for
the spending summary and \mathrm{int} for the interaction view.
Final adapters are fitted offline before Period 1; a weekly
build is released with them only if it passes the compatibility checks
(Section 4.2).
Starting from precomputed base scores, the online path scores a
1,000-transaction CPU batch in 1–2 ms, with no LLM call or nearest-neighbor
search (Section 5.5).

sections.name: Evaluation
sections.text:
Following the setup in Section 5.1, we address four research
questions (RQs) in Sections 5.2–5.5. RQ1 asks
whether PersonaAgent improves all four frozen detectors, offline and in
deployment. RQ2 asks how informative the persona views and semantic topics are,
RQ3 which alerts the final score would change in deployment, and RQ4 how
efficient and robust PersonaAgent is in operation.

sections.name: Evaluation Setup
sections.text:
To evaluate the contribution of persona memory to detectors already in use,
we compare each detector’s final score with its own frozen base score. The
comparison measures score quality, not authorization decisions. The BM1
operating-point rule was fixed before Period 1 and is applied unchanged to the
base and final scores in both periods.
Table 2 separates protocol design and adapter
fitting from the two evaluation periods. Period 1 is a held-out offline test;
Period 2 scored live traffic before any outcome was known, and outcomes were
joined later. The memory snapshot and four adapters frozen before Period 1 stay
unchanged through Period 2, which tests whether gains over the frozen
detectors persist as the memory ages without weekly refresh.

sections.name: RQ1: Does PersonaAgent Improve Four Frozen Detectors?
sections.text:
The release package improves every detector on every metric in both periods.
Table 3 reports relative improvements over each
frozen detector: all 24 detector–period–metric comparisons show improvements, and
every 95% confidence interval lies above zero. These intervals are computed
with a paired bootstrap over transactions (Appendix F).

All 24 comparisons also show improvements when the fusion network is refitted on the
same data with five random seeds. Protocol search used only
Detector 4 feedback, so Detectors 1–3 test transfer of the selected
protocol. Detector 2 achieves the largest gain on the selection metric BM1 in
both periods, showing that the protocol’s benefit extends beyond the detector
used to select it.

In deployment, BM1 improves by a relative 8.93–14.24%, while the
threshold-free PR-AUC and AUC improve by 0.65–6.58% and 0.23–0.66%,
respectively. The gains therefore extend from the deployed operating point to
both ranking metrics, with smaller relative improvements in AUC.

From Period 1 to Period 2, relative improvements fall in eight of the twelve
detector–metric combinations, are unchanged in one, and rise in three. The
relative improvement in BM1 falls for Detectors 1, 2, and 4 but more than doubles for
Detector 3 (Appendix F). The unchanged release
package nonetheless improves all four frozen detectors in
Period 2.

sections.name: Contribution of persona views.
sections.text:
RQ1 shows that the release package improves every detector; RQ2 first uses
matched ablations to assess what the five persona views add to the adapter
beyond its base-score inputs. Each variant refits the fusion network on the
same training rows, changing only its inputs, and scores the transactions of
both periods offline (Appendix F). With the frozen base score as its only
input, the refit adapter leaves PR-AUC and AUC unchanged (0.00% relative improvement) for every
detector in both periods. A second variant adds the metadata-adjusted base score
but none of the five persona views; it slightly reduces PR-AUC for
Detectors 1–3 and gives a +1.17\% relative improvement for
Detector 4. Adding the five persona
views to this second variant increases the relative improvements in PR-AUC and AUC by 3.20 and
0.44 percentage points on average, and PR-AUC, AUC, and BM1 all rise in each of
the eight detector–period combinations.

sections.name: Standalone view prediction.
sections.text:
We next assess the information in each view alone. Each single-view
predictor scores transactions from one persona view, without the base score or
the fusion network, on a pre-release memory snapshot built under the released
package’s protocol and topic definitions. Both figures report
normalized strength: a predictor’s AUC above chance,
\mathrm{AUC}-0.5 , divided by that of a reference predictor. Here the reference
is the spending summary in Period 1; the topic comparison below uses a
different reference, so values should be compared within each figure.
All five views predict anomalies above chance in both periods, and their
ranking holds as the memory ages: the spending summary first, followed by
Merchant topics (Fig. 5). The top-ranked spending
summary itself draws on the topics: it records the card’s shares of eligible
historical activity across Merchant, MCC, and Location topics, such as its
share in the MCC topic for airline and cruise travel
(Appendix C). The interaction predictor ranks slightly
above the MCC predictor and well above the Location predictor in both periods,
so joint MCC-topic–Location-topic context, kept for supported pairs
(Section 4.2), predicts better than either topic alone.

sections.name: Semantic topics versus conventional clustering.
sections.text:
We finally assess the hierarchical topic grouping as a whole by comparing the
topics selected at design time with conventional clustering for the Merchant,
MCC, Location, and interaction views. Conventional clustering forms groups
directly from numerical features without narrative embeddings or
agent-formulated topic definitions. Both groupings use the same held-out
Period 1 transactions, numbers of groups, single-view predictor, and evaluation
procedure, and each derives its interaction view from its own MCC and Location
groups. The selected scheme follows the hierarchical construction of
Section 4.1: agent-formulated MCC and Location topics, mapped in
Fig. 3, with Merchant topics formed by behavior-feature
clustering within the MCC topics. In standalone prediction, the selected topic
scheme outperforms matched conventional clustering for three of the four group
views (Fig. 6). Here normalized strength uses the semantic
Merchant-topic predictor’s AUC above chance as its reference. On this scale,
semantic topics lead by +0.26 on MCC (about a quarter
of the reference’s AUC above chance), +0.19 on Merchant, and +0.14 on the
interaction view; Location scores are nearly equal.

sections.name: RQ3: Which Alerts Would the Final Score Change in Deployment?
sections.text:
RQ3 examines individual alert changes in addition to aggregate metrics. The
base and final scores were recorded live in Period 2, before outcomes were
known. Once outcomes became available, we reconstructed alerts from those
recorded scores using the same BM1 operating-point rule fixed before
Period 1, with a separate analysis threshold determined for each score.
Compared with the base score’s alerts, the final score can recover a missed
anomaly (a recovery), withdraw a false alert, introduce a false alert,
or lose a detected anomaly (a lost detection). The relative improvements in BM1 in
Table 3, measured at this same operating point, show
the combined effect of these four changes.

Recovered anomalies are largely detector-specific: of the distinct anomalies
recovered for at least one detector in Period 2, 71.7% are recovered for
exactly one detector and 10.6% for three or more. To compare correction
patterns across periods, we use a detector’s correction fingerprint,
which contrasts its recovered anomalies with its lost detections on
characteristics that include the five persona-view scores. For every
detector, the Period 1 and Period 2 fingerprints have a cosine similarity of
at least 0.93, indicating similar patterns of relative differences in these characteristics across periods (Appendix F).
Table 4 illustrates these corrections with two
recovered anomalies and two withdrawn false alerts from Period 2, with
persona-view scores given as percentiles (pct).

In three of the four cases (rows one, three, and four), the alert changes are
consistent with the card’s spending-summary scores despite contrasting
group-view scores. Rows two and three share a Merchant-topic record and a Merchant-view
score at pct90, but have different spending-summary scores and opposite alert
changes: row two, with a mid-range spending-summary score (pct49), is a
recovered anomaly, whereas row three, with a low score (pct3), is a withdrawn
false alert. The anomaly in row one is recovered despite low group-view scores,
while the false alert in row four is withdrawn despite high group-view scores. Their
spending-summary scores are pct99 and pct7, respectively; the transaction
amount is below the Merchant topic’s usual level in row one and far above it
in row four.

sections.name: RQ4: How Efficient and Robust Is PersonaAgent in Operation?
sections.text:
We measure serving cost and performance under sparse history, then describe
how scoring and refresh handle failures.

sections.name: Serving cost.
sections.text:
On CPU, the online path scores a batch of 1,000 transactions in 1–2 ms,
measured from receiving the transactions and their frozen base scores to
returning final scores; this covers lookup, feature-vector construction, the
five encoders, and
the fusion of Eq. 1. Adding another detector reuses the
shared memory build and requires its own adapter fit; fitting one adapter took
approximately 20–48 minutes.

sections.name: Sparse history.
sections.text:
On transactions served by MCC-topic fallback (Appendix C),
such as those at previously unseen Merchants, the mean relative improvement in PR-AUC across the four detectors is 3.30% and 3.64% in Periods 1 and 2. All 24 detector–period–metric comparisons show improvements with
confidence intervals above zero when the comparison in Table 3 is
recomputed on this subset. These results address the long-tail case raised in
Section 1.

sections.name: Failure handling.
sections.text:
Failures in PersonaAgent’s path do not stop scoring. A serving failure, such
as an unavailable lookup, returns the frozen base score; a failed refresh
validation leaves the previous package active, so scoring continues with
the existing memory. Figure 7 shows release control and
request serving, and Appendix Table 5 gives the
corresponding controls.

sections.name: Design principles.
sections.text:
Compatibility with an existing adapter requires stable topic meanings as well
as stable input dimensions. The spending summary, for example, stores a card’s
share of past activity in each topic. If a topic ID were reused for different
behavior, the adapter would still accept its inputs but misread them: a card’s
share of the redefined topic would count as its share of the original one.
Topic identity therefore belongs in release checks alongside schema and
fallback. The validated release package is the unit of activation, maintenance,
and rollback, allowing entity knowledge to be updated independently of each
detector’s release cycle. This separates scheduled knowledge construction from
serving activation: a weekly build produces a candidate memory, but activation
requires a validated package rather than a new detector release.

sections.name: Scope and future directions.
sections.text:
The record-age comparison shows that the relative improvement in BM1 is
lower for every detector
when MCC-topic, Location-topic, and interaction records come from the
preceding weekly build (Appendix F). This sensitivity to
record age motivates a direct comparison of weekly refresh with a fixed
release package. Versioned releases allow the refresh frequency to be varied,
so the performance benefit of fresher records can be evaluated against rebuild
and validation cost.
Location-derived signals may correlate with sensitive attributes, so
subgroup-impact assessment should precede policy-level use.

sections.name: Conclusion
sections.text:
PersonaAgent addresses the knowledge-latency gap between weekly re-estimation
of entity behavior and months-long detector release cycles. It keeps behavioral
context in a shared, refreshable persona memory outside the detectors,
organized by semantic topics that pool evidence for rare and cold-start
entities. At design time, the protocol for building this memory evolves through
a bounded agentic search: LLM roles propose revisions, and a prespecified rule
selects the protocol to freeze. Online, deterministic retrieval and
detector-specific adapters link the memory to frozen detectors without LLM
calls. One release package, unchanged across both periods, improved every reported
metric for four detectors offline and in deployment, where the production
business metric (BM1) rose by a relative 8.93–14.24%. New behavioral evidence
can reach several deployed detectors through one validated release package,
without waiting for any detector’s next release.

sections.name: Adapter architecture and fitting.
sections.text:
Each persona view contributes one encoder
output; the original and metadata-adjusted base scores supply the other two
inputs. We use tree-based encoders and an MLP fusion network because trees
remain strong on tabular data (Chen and Guestrin, 2016; Grinsztajn et al., 2022) and
tree/MLP hybrids are effective (Yan et al., 2024). The deterministic fusion
network contains hundreds
of parameters, excluding the tree-based encoders. In Eq. 1, each
encoder output is first clipped slightly away from 0 and 1 so that its logit is
finite. Final adapters are fitted and selected using eligible outcomes and
cutoff-valid persona feature vectors. The fusion network is trained on
out-of-fold encoder predictions: we
split the training rows into five parts and predict each part with encoders
fitted on the other four.

sections.name: Memory construction.
sections.text:
At cutoff T , the weekly build of Section 4.2 computes the
memory

that is, the build \mathcal{C} applies the frozen protocol \Pi^{\star} , with
its fixed topic definitions, under the execution configuration E^{\star} to the
eligible historical transactions \mathcal{X}_{T} observed by T and their
outcomes \mathcal{Y}_{T} available by T . Algorithm 2 writes
D_{T} for this evidence and K_{T}^{\mathrm{cand}} for the snapshot before
validation.
The five views are indexed by \mathcal{L}=\{\mathrm{cb,mer,mcc,loc,int}\} , and
the topic scheme has three families,
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{topic}}=\{\mathrm{mer,mcc,loc}\} .
The spending summary covers the card’s own history over these topics; the
interaction
view uses supported MCC-topic–Location-topic pairs. All five views
and their topic-assignment maps share this cutoff.

sections.name: Retrieval keys.
sections.text:
Online retrieval uses exact-key lookup over a versioned snapshot rather than
nearest-neighbor search. Using a snapshot built at cutoff T , the system
resolves five logical keys for transaction x , one per view
(Fig. 2(C)):

The spending summary is keyed by the card itself; Merchant, MCC, and Location
fields resolve through the topic-assignment maps, and
k_{\mathrm{int},T}(x)=\big(k_{\mathrm{mcc},T}(x),k_{\mathrm{loc},T}(x)\big)
is the resolved MCC-topic–Location-topic pair.

fallback map
\beta_{\ell,T(x)} , and \operatorname{Project} returns a fixed-length feature
vector:
each view’s record values and reliability indicators, plus the three activity
shares the resolved topic IDs select from the spending summary. Its length never

sections.name: Fallback rules.
sections.text:
A group must meet the protocol’s minimum support requirement to have its own
record; otherwise, \operatorname{LookupOrFallback} follows
\beta_{\ell,T(x)} , which the snapshot stores, to a record for a larger group.
A
Merchant without a supported topic mapping uses its parent MCC-topic fallback
record for the Merchant view, while the MCC view is still read separately with
the MCC-topic key; this fills the Merchant view without assigning the Merchant
to a Merchant topic. The metadata input for such a Merchant uses the parent
MCC-topic reference. If an MCC-topic–Location-topic pair has too little
history, the interaction view uses a predefined record for one of the two
topics (a marginal record), such as the MCC topic, or a fixed missing-value
record if no such record is available. Each view keeps its fixed schema, and
the fallback level (exact, parent, marginal, or missing) tells the adapter what
evidence was available. Sparse history is therefore handled by fallback; only a
serving failure returns the frozen base score. Algorithm 3
gives the scoring pseudocode, including how
such failures are handled. Section 5.5 shows that the gain holds on
transactions served by MCC-topic fallback.

sections.name: An illustrative revision.
sections.text:
Consider a candidate narrative schema N that permits an interpretation such
as issuer caution is visible in lower approval. A lower approval rate is
an observed comparison; it does not establish issuer intent. The Protocol Critic
could diagnose this explanation as unsupported.
The Narrative Schema role could then revise N to require an observed
field-and-baseline comparison without attributing intent. The resulting
description would state approval is below its overall baseline.
This would change the rule governing subsequent narratives, not just one
sentence; it would not by itself change topic membership.
A better-grounded description is not sufficient for acceptance. A candidate replaces
the current best protocol only if development BM1 improves and the prespecified
checks pass; a
source-consistent candidate without improvement is rejected, as is an
improving candidate that fails a required check. The critic’s diagnosis guides
the next proposal but cannot override that rule.

sections.name: After the protocol is frozen.
sections.text:
Newly eligible history supplies updated numerical evidence, and the build
applies the fixed topic definitions and topic-assignment rules to construct
records and
maps. For a previously unseen Merchant
without a supported mapping, the predefined parent MCC-topic fallback supplies
the context, with fallback level and support passed to the adapter.

sections.name: Fixed search inputs.
sections.text:
The evaluation procedure H , selection rule
g_{\mathrm{dev}} , and search budget are fixed inputs, not outputs of an LLM
role. Each candidate’s G specifies its release checks; revisions to G are
themselves evaluated under the same H and g_{\mathrm{dev}} .
The execution configuration E^{\star} records software and execution settings
separately from the selected protocol. It pins the generator and embedding
configuration, which are reproducible internally but unnamed under our
disclosure policy.

For each candidate, H rebuilds memory, fits a temporary adapter around frozen
Detector 4, and reports development BM1 and check results; the temporary
adapters are not released. The selection rule
decides acceptance; \mathrm{ProtocolDiff} records the changed components.
The log retains proposals, diagnoses, and decisions.

Each weekly run of Algorithm 2 updates all five numerical views
under the selected topic
definitions; it does not repeat protocol search. The complete package is
activated in one switch, and a failed validation leaves the prior package active.

The serving procedure (Algorithm 3) uses explicit safe exits so
scoring can continue when PersonaAgent’s serving path fails. If package
pinning, key resolution, record retrieval, feature-vector construction,
metadata derivation, or adapter execution fails, the transaction retains the
frozen detector’s original score.

sections.name: Confidence intervals and refits.
sections.text:
The intervals in Table 3 come from a paired bootstrap
over transactions. Within each period, each of 1,000 draws resamples
transactions with replacement, keeping each transaction’s label and its base and
final scores together, and recomputes every relative improvement; the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles
of the draws give the interval. The same draws serve all four detectors and all three
metrics within a period. To measure fitting variability, we refit the fusion
network with five seeds while keeping persona records, view encoders, base
scores, and data fixed. All 24 comparisons show improvements in every refit, and the
standard deviation of the relative improvement across seeds, averaged over the eight detector–period
cells, is 1.21 (BM1), 0.15 (PR-AUC), and 0.013 (AUC) percentage points.

sections.name: Cross-period performance.
sections.text:
Both periods evaluate the same adapters, frozen before Period 1. From Period 1
to Period 2, the relative improvement in BM1 decreases by approximately two-fifths for Detector 1
and nearly three-tenths for Detector 2, while it more than doubles for Detector 3
(Table 3). The gains vary across detectors and
metrics but remain positive in Period 2.

sections.name: Record age.
sections.text:
To test whether fresher records matter, we rescore Period 2 after replacing
only the frozen package’s MCC-topic, Location-topic, and interaction records
with those of the preceding weekly build. The protocol, encoders, and adapters
remain fixed within each comparison. The package’s own, fresher records give
a higher relative improvement in BM1 for every detector, by 0.86, 0.78, 2.52, and 0.82 percentage points averaged over seeds for Detectors 1–4, and the difference is positive in every seed. The relative improvement in PR-AUC is higher by 0.16, 0.25, and 0.28 percentage points for Detectors 1–3
and unchanged for Detector 4; the relative improvement in AUC changes by at most 0.02 percentage points.

sections.name: Matched ablations.
sections.text:
The matched ablations in Section 5.3 refit the fusion network on the
same training rows with the same architecture and fitting procedure, changing
only its inputs: the base score alone; the base score and the metadata-adjusted
base score; or these two scores with the five view predictions, as in
Eq. 1.
Variants with views reuse the same out-of-fold encoder predictions. Each variant
scores the transactions of both periods offline, and reported values average
three random seeds; differences between variants are in percentage points of
relative improvement.

sections.name: Correction-fingerprint diagnostic.
sections.text:
We define a correction fingerprint for each detector and period
as a seven-dimensional effect-size vector contrasting recovered anomalies with
lost detections. Recovered anomalies are confirmed anomalies flagged
only by PersonaAgent; lost detections are confirmed anomalies flagged only by
the frozen detector. Both cohorts use the retrospective analysis thresholds of
Section 5.4. The seven features are the five persona-view scores,
transaction amount, and Merchant-topic-relative amount. For each feature,
Cliff’s delta is the fraction of recovered/lost pairs where the recovered
transaction’s value is higher minus the fraction where it is lower. Missing
values are omitted separately by feature. These seven signed effects form the
correction fingerprint, and its cosine similarity across periods is near 1 when
they keep the same signs and relative sizes in both periods.
